stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
stimulus:
Trees in cooler climates tend to have leaves with toothed rather than smooth edges, so paleobotanists often estimate past temperatures from the percentage of toothed-margin species in a fossil flora. Paleobotanist Ines Haldane cautions that the method can mislead. Plants along streams root in wet, frequently disturbed soils; such soils favor fast-growing species; and fast-growing species are disproportionately toothed. A streamside setting, Haldane argues, can therefore raise a flora's toothed percentage even when temperature does not differ. For example, ______

Four Fossil Floras
Flora | Setting | Temperature from isotope data (°C) | Toothed-margin species (%)
P | Streamside | 18 | 41
Q | Upland lake | 18 | 27
R | Streamside | 14 | 55
S | Upland lake | 14 | 38
choices: Flora P (streamside, 18°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora R (streamside, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora R (streamside, 14°C) did.
explanation: Work out what the example has to show before you read the choices. Haldane's claim has a scope phrase: a streamside setting raises the toothed percentage 'even when temperature does not differ.' So the example has to compare a streamside flora with a non-streamside flora at the same temperature, and the streamside flora has to have the higher percentage. Floras P and Q were both 18°C, P is streamside, and P has 41% against Q's 27%. Setting is the only thing that differs between them, so the difference can be put down to setting.

B.why: This is the second-order trap. You saw correctly that the example needs streamside versus non-streamside, and R (55%) is higher than Q (27%). But R is also 4°C cooler than Q, and cooler climates have more toothed species anyway. The gap could come entirely from temperature, so it doesn't show what setting does when temperature is held equal.

C.why: This reading is accurate: S (38%) is higher than Q (27%). But both floras come from upland lakes. The only difference is temperature, so this shows the familiar temperature effect, not Haldane's point about streamside settings. You picked a true comparison that doesn't prove the passage's claim.

D.why: You picked the right kind of pair (same temperature, different setting) but got the direction backwards. At 14°C, streamside Flora R has 55% and upland-lake Flora S has 38%, so S is lower than R. The choice misreads the table, and the comparison it states would actually count against Haldane's claim.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
stimulus: City planners often widen sidewalks by narrowing traffic lanes, expecting the added room to draw more pedestrians. In hot months, however, unshaded concrete absorbs heat, and hot pavement discourages walking, so extra sidewalk space may attract few people unless something keeps it cool. After studying 40 downtown blocks from 2023 to 2025, urban planner Tomás Reyes-Whitfield concluded that widening sidewalks increased summer afternoon foot traffic only on blocks where street trees shaded the sidewalk. For example, ______

figure.caption: Change in Summer Afternoon Foot Traffic on 40 Downtown Blocks, 2023–2025
figure.alt: Bar graph of the percent change in summer afternoon pedestrian counts for four block types: widened and shaded, unwidened and shaded, widened and unshaded, and unwidened and unshaded. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 28 percent in steps of 4.

choices: widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened and unwidened unshaded blocks each gained 4%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for widened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for unwidened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened, unshaded blocks gained more than unwidened ones.
explanation: The word 'only' means the example has to show two things. First, among shaded blocks, widening raised foot traffic: widened blocks gained 24% and unwidened blocks gained 8%. Second, among unshaded blocks, widening made no difference: widened and unwidened blocks both gained 4%. Choice A is the only option that states both comparisons, each with shade held constant. Together they show that widening helped where there was shade and did not help where there wasn't.

B.why: These numbers are read correctly, but the main comparison (24% versus 4%) is between two widened blocks that differ in shade. That shows shade matters once a sidewalk is widened. It doesn't show what widening does on unshaded blocks, because there's no unwidened, unshaded baseline. The 4% could still be a gain caused by widening, so 'only on shaded blocks' isn't established.

C.why: Comparing widened, shaded blocks (24%) with unwidened, unshaded blocks (4%) changes two things at once. The gap could come from widening, from shade, or from both, so it can't show that widening works only where there is shade. You went with the biggest gap on the graph instead of a comparison that isolates widening.

D.why: This choice starts with the right comparison, which is why it's tempting once you've found the key idea. But it finishes by misreading the graph: widened and unwidened unshaded blocks both gained 4%, so neither gained more. And if widening had helped unshaded blocks, that would undercut the word 'only' in the claim rather than support it.
